soil-form-102.title: Bedrock, the solid floor beneath the soil
soil-form-102.text: Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the spade strikes solid rock. Bedrock is that solid rock, lying beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits in the crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet. Where it breaks the surface, the exposed patch is an outcrop. Its buried top, where it meets the material above, is the rockhead. Locating rockhead by digging, drilling or geophysics matters in most civil engineering projects, and it can lie hundreds of metres down. Exposed bedrock weathers physically or chemically and then erodes. At its buried upper boundary, weathering below ground turns it into {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Fragments torn from it and found higher up, among the weathered layers and soil, are called floaters. Geological maps show bedrock as if every soil and {{ref:soil-form-103}} had been stripped away, unless the cover is too thick to map through. In mapping such cover, every deposit older than the Quaternary counts as bedrock.

soil-form-097.title: Regolith, the loose blanket over solid rock
soil-form-097.text: Few plants can grow in solid rock, and animals need loose material to burrow. Most life on land therefore rests on regolith: a blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock. George P. Merrill coined the word in 1897 from the Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock. He meant the whole mantle of loose material, whatever its origin. It includes dust, broken rock and related materials. It occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons. On Earth it comes from weathering and biological processes, and it ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick. Its age varies just as widely. Fresh volcanic ash or river sediment is instantly regolith, while parts of Australia carry Precambrian regolith hundreds of millions of years old. The blanket has several ingredients: transported cover, deeply weathered rock, interbedded volcanic deposits, hard crusts, groundwater salts and living things. Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil. Regolith matters well beyond biology. Engineers build on it, mineral deposits lie in it, and it supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum. It is also the zone through which underground water stores recharge and discharge.

soil-form-100.title: Saprolite, the rotten rock that keeps its shape
soil-form-100.text: Saprolite means rotten rock. It is chemically weathered rock, formed in the lower zones of soil profiles as weathering eats deep into the bedrock surface. It commonly keeps the structural details of its bedrock. It also inherits that rock's texture, pH and minerals. Hydrolysis, {{ref:soil-chem-069}}, hydration and freeze–thaw turn granite and other rocks into it. Quartz resists the attack and can be left behind as sandy soil, a process called arenization. Iron compounds supply most of its color. One, {{ref:soil-chem-104}}, is yellow when fine and brown when coarse. Another, {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, is red when fine and grey to black when coarse. Upper saprolite is fully oxidized bedrock, and lower saprolite is reduced, partly weathered rock. Below lies saprock, bedrock weathered only along its fractures. Younger than its parent rock and older than any thick cover such as lava, saprolite can sometimes be dated relatively. Burrowing plants and animals bring it up to the surface. In Western Australia, poorly weathered saprolite grit forms aquifers that can yield groundwater fit for livestock.

soil-form-098.title: Asteroid regolith, soil-like dust on tiny worlds
soil-form-098.text: Asteroids wear loose blankets too. Asteroid regolith is the loose surface layer of an asteroid, produced by impacts and other processes that alter its surface. Spacecraft show it ranging from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris. The Hayabusa mission's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in a laboratory. They showed space weathering and particles implanted by the solar wind. Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020, and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023. Both hold organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

soil-form-099.title: Titan, where ice behaves like rock
soil-form-099.text: On Saturn's moon Titan, ice does the job of rock. The word regolith traditionally covered only loose mineral grains or rock fragments. Ice grains were left out because, like snow on Earth, they melt and fuse easily. Titan is so cold that ice behaves like rock, with its own erosion and its own wind-driven and sedimentary processes. Its loose icy material behaves mechanically like regolith elsewhere, so it earns the name. Data from an instrument the Huygens probe pushed into the ground suggest a sand of ice grains on a plain of somewhat rounded pebbles.

soil-form-101.title: Deep weathering, rock rotting for millions of years
soil-form-101.text: At 20 m per million years, weathering needs several million years to build a deep regolith, and cooler climates need longer. Deep weathering is that long-continued chemical attack. It builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history. Three conditions favor it. Relief must be gentle enough to prevent erosion and let water carry dissolved material down. The crust must stay tectonically stable for a long time. The climate must be humid, tropical to temperate, with warmth to speed the reactions. Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S. In parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia, regolith has been forming for over 100 million years. Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock. The process sorts the elements as it goes. Sulfides and carbonates leave readily. Nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc held in iron- and magnesium-rich minerals stay higher. They reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in the middle and lower saprolite. The result is secondary and supergene ores, enriched near the surface by weathering: {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual heavy minerals. Sweden shows the process across deep time. There it formed thin clay-rich saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago.

soil-form-103.title: Superficial deposits, the young loose cover
soil-form-103.text: Most of the loose ground people walk on is geologically young. Superficial deposits are recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age, less than 2.6 million years old. They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, glacial drift and moraine, raised beaches and {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Most are gravel, sand, silt and clay. Onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches. Geological surveys keep databases of their properties. Farmers and foresters use them to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrients washing out.

soil-form-087.title: Parent material, the stuff every soil grows from
soil-form-087.text: Every soil carries a family likeness to the material it grew from. Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon. Parent material is the underlying geological material in which soil horizons form, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit. It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock. For a metamorphic rock, the original rock before it changed is the protolith. It may also be loose glacial, river or volcanic deposits. Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and the mica called biotite. The parent leaves a clear mark. Mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils. Parent material also strongly shapes how many basic ions a soil contains. Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favor one kind of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, called mull, while a shortage of them goes with another, called moder. Soil scientists sort parent materials by how they were deposited. Residual material weathered in place. Transported material was carried by water, wind, ice or gravity. Cumulose material is organic matter that accumulated where it formed. Because soils inherit so much of their structure and minerals from their parent, they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.

soil-form-089.title: Transported parent material, soil from somewhere else
soil-form-089.text: Most soils form in material that wind, water, ice and gravity have carried many miles. Transported parent material is loose, uncemented material moved this way, and it is named for its last means of transport. Material a glacier carried and streams then redeposited counts as stream-transported, or glacial fluvial, parent material. The recognized carriers are wind, water, gravity, ice, lakes and oceans, and the entries ahead give each deposit its name. Water-carried material is split three ways: by rivers, in lakes or in the sea. Wind sorts its load. It moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to build {{ref:soil-form-106}}. It seldom moves clay, which sticks into stable clumps. Wind also piles sand-sized grains into dunes and drops volcanic ash at various distances from a volcano. In the field, rock fragments that thin out with depth, especially over saprolite, suggest the soil material has moved downslope.

soil-form-106.title: Loess, the wind-blown silt that buries whole regions
soil-form-106.text: Ten percent of Earth's land lies under loess or similar deposits. Loess is a clastic sediment, built of fragments, that is mostly silt-sized and formed by the build-up of wind-blown dust. It holds 20% or less clay, with roughly equal parts sand and silt, typically 20 to 50 micrometres across. Calcium carbonate often cements it loosely. It is even-textured, porous, crumbly, pale yellow or buff and usually unlayered. Its angular grains of quartz, feldspar and mica let it stand in vertical banks. In parts of China people dig cave dwellings into them. Deposits exceed a hundred metres in north-western China, reaching 350 m on the {{ref:soil-form-110}}, and run tens of metres thick in the US Midwest. Pye in 1995 listed four requirements: a dust source, enough wind to carry it, a place to accumulate, and time. Von Leonhard described Löss along the Rhine in 1823–1824, and Lyell popularized the term in 1834. Its wind-blown origin was recognized later, notably by von Richthofen in China in 1878.

soil-form-112.title: Alluvium, the sediment that rivers leave behind
soil-form-112.text: Some of the earliest human civilizations grew on river mud. Alluvium is loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in alluvial fans or similar settings. Floodplain alluvium can be highly fertile. It is usually geologically young and unconsolidated, and most of it is Quaternary. It is often called cover, because it hides the bedrock beneath. Running water sorts what it drops, so alluvium is generally fine-grained and well sorted. Seasonal floods leave it in layers on floodplains. Alluvial fans coarsen toward the uplands, and deltas at river mouths are fine-grained. Sediment laid down in seas, estuaries, lakes or ponds is not called alluvium. Beyond that, geologists still disagree over which other deposits the term should include. The word is old. Antoine Furetière's dictionary, published in 1690, defined alluvion as new land formed by sediment along rivers and seas. In the 19th century alluvium meant river sediment lying above older diluvium, which was ascribed to Noah's flood. Once that idea was rejected, diluvium became older alluvium.

soil-form-113.title: Colluvium, the jumble at the foot of the slope
soil-form-113.text: At the base of a hillslope, debris gathers. Colluvium is loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited there by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a mix of these. It is a varied blend of rock types and sizes, from silt to rock fragments, typically angular and loosely consolidated. It builds gently sloping aprons or fans at the foot of slopes, or fills gullies and hollows, sometimes several metres thick. Where gravity moves material, talus cones at the base of steep slopes make it obvious. Unlike alluvium, colluvium involves no running water, so it is poorly sorted where alluvium is well sorted. Where the source material is fine and uniform, though, it can be hard to tell which process laid a deposit down. Thick colluvium often holds buried soils, plant and animal remains and archaeological deposits. Together they record long-term climatic change.

soil-form-110.title: The Loess Plateau, China's yellow highland
soil-form-110.text: The Yellow River owes its name and its color to the loess in its banks. Around the river's upper and middle reaches lies the Loess Plateau, some 640,000 km2 covered by loess. It holds the thickest known loess deposit, up to 350 m. Farmed for over a thousand years, it has produced phenomenal yields. Yet its soil has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth. Wind-borne loess particles from it add to the Asian Dust pollution problem.

soil-form-109.title: Why loess soils are so fertile and so fragile
soil-form-109.text: Soils developed on loess tend to be very rich. Under suitable climates they rank among the most agriculturally productive in the world. Their fine grains weather quickly because of their large surface area. Their fertility comes mainly from {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and its many pores, not from organic matter. Soils underlain by loess also tend to drain too freely. Their weakness is erosion. Even well-managed loess farmland can lose well over 2.5 kg/m2 a year. Under autumn moldboard plowing, Iowa's Loess Hills at times lost over 10 kg/m2 a year. Their fertility rests on 10,000 years of dark prairie organic matter. Once that surface layer erodes, the loess beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

soil-form-111.title: Loess–paleosol sequences, climate diaries in silt
soil-form-111.text: Some loess cliffs read like a climate diary. Their stacked layers of loess, separated by buried soils, form loess–paleosol sequences studied as archives of past climate and environmental change. In China a strong north-west winter monsoon laid down the loess layers. The buried soils record a moist south-east monsoon. Without robust numerical dating, even the place of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess was long debated. Since the 1980s, luminescence methods have dated when grains last saw daylight. SAR protocols give last-glacial ages accurate to between 5 and 10%. Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages for the last 40–45 ka, or thousand years, when charcoal or snail shells lie in place.

soil-form-108.title: Non-glacial loess, dust from deserts and volcanoes
soil-form-108.text: Not all loess owes its origin to ice. Non-glacial loess comes from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or volcanic ash, not from the sediment washed out of glaciers. Desert loess forms as wind-driven quartz grains abrade one another. Volcanic loess occurs in Ecuador and Argentina, and there are tropical and trade-wind kinds too. China's thick loess deposits blew in from deserts in the north of the country. Loess on the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Colorado is considered non-glacial desert loess, as is loess in Australia and Africa.

soil-form-088.title: Residuum, weathered rock that never moved
soil-form-088.text: In the United States as little as three percent of soils are residual. Residuum is weathered rock that stays in place instead of being moved by erosion, and in time it helps form soil. It is purely mineral, unlike organic parent materials, and wind, water and gravity have not moved it. Soils formed from it, residual soils, should resemble their underlying bedrock in mineralogy and general chemistry. They imply a stable landscape, which explains their rarity. Regolith covers all loose material above bedrock, transported sediment included, while residuum is strictly untransported. Saprolite keeps its bedrock's structure. Residuum has lost it, transformed further and shrunk in volume. It forms mainly by chemical weathering in every climate, as a thin blanket over bedrock in temperate regions and much thicker in the tropics. On limestone the boundary with bedrock is sharp but irregular. Pinnacles of fresh rock rise into reddish residual silts and clays, and resistant chert or sandstone remains as float.

soil-form-105.title: Eluvial deposits, the riches weathering leaves behind
soil-form-105.text: Brazil's Pitinga tin deposit, one of the largest tin mines in the world, is what weathering left behind. In geology, eluvial deposits are deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus movement or accumulation by gravity. What was removed is irrelevant; the eluvial deposit is what remains. Winnowing away lighter material enriches eluvial ores such as tungsten and gold placers, concentrations of heavy grains. Diamonds in weathered kimberlite can count as eluvial too. In Ontario, supergene weathering of an apatite-rich carbonatite rock produced a significant eluvial phosphate ore.

soil-form-090.title: Glacial till, the unsorted load a glacier drops
soil-form-090.text: A boulder in a field may have come from an outcrop hundreds of kilometres away. Glacial till is unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice. No liquid water carried it, so it is unsorted and unlayered. It is mostly clay, silt and sand with scattered pebbles, cobbles and boulders, often in a bimodal size distribution with two peaks. Its stones are often faceted, scratched or polished by glacial abrasion. Basal till, laid beneath the glacier, is typically very compact and slow to take in water. Ablation till, dropped as the ice melts, is less compacted. Till forms terminal, lateral, medial and ground moraines, and the ridges called drumlins and flutes. Archibald Geikie first applied the term to primary glacial deposits in 1863. The older name, boulder clay, has fallen out of favor. Melting glaciers rework till into outwash and into lake or sea deposits such as varves.

soil-form-095.title: Cumulose parent material, soil built from plants
soil-form-095.text: Not every parent material is rock. Cumulose parent material is organic, built up in place from plant residues such as sphagnum moss. Groundwater standing high keeps oxygen low, which slows decay and preserves the residues. {{ref:soil-class-070}} and muck soils both form this way. Unlike other parent materials, it is never moved; it originates from organic material deposited where it lies. The results differ sharply. The first may form sterile soils, while muck soils may be very fertile.

soil-form-091.title: Glaciofluvial deposits, ice debris sorted by meltwater
soil-form-091.text: Meltwater sorts what the ice did not. Glaciofluvial deposits are boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited. They are laid down beside, below or downstream from the ice. Retreating glaciers leave outwash plains as this sediment is carried downstream. Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

soil-form-107.title: Periglacial loess, dust from dried-out meltwater rivers
soil-form-107.text: Each autumn and winter, the meltwater flowing from the great ice sheets dwindled. Bare floodplains of braided rivers dried, and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, dropping it downwind. The result is periglacial loess: loess blown from the floodplains of rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps. The loess along both sides of the Mississippi River alluvial valley is a classic example. The northern European loess belt, from southern England to southern Ukraine, shows strong periglacial influence. In England it has its own name, {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Loess ridges aligned with last-glacial winds are called paha ridges in America and greda ridges in Europe.

soil-form-093.title: Lacustrine parent material, the silt of old lakebeds
soil-form-093.text: Lake Bonneville and many soils around the Great Lakes share an origin in still water. Lacustrine parent material is sediment that settled in lakes. It forms a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay. Its high clay content makes the soils formed in it let water through only slowly. Beach ridges may mark where ancient lakes once washed up sand.

soil-form-092.title: Glaciolacustrine deposits and the yearly layers of varves
soil-form-092.text: Lakes at the edge of an ice sheet collect what glaciers shed. Glaciolacustrine deposits are parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin. Inflowing rivers drop their larger rocks and stones near the lake edge. Their suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed. Annual deposition can leave clear layers called varves.

soil-form-094.title: Marine parent material, old sea floors turned to soil
soil-form-094.text: Parts of the US Gulf Coast were once sea bed. Marine parent material is material that rivers carried to the sea, where it sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material. Soils along the Gulf Coast and in California's Imperial Valley formed on such ancient sea beds, exposed as the land was uplifted. Glaciomarine sediments reached the ocean by glacier or iceberg. They may hold large ice-dropped boulders amid fine-grained sediment.

soil-form-096.title: Volcanic ash, a fast-weathering parent material
soil-form-096.text: Volcanic ash is made largely of glass, and it weathers fast. Ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano is called tephra, the most common volcanic parent material. Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with loose material are part of Earth's regolith. Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with a high internal surface area. They weather rapidly to the clay minerals {{ref:soil-chem-098}} and {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. These soils, classed as {{ref:soil-class-092}}, are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and particularly light for their volume. Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

soil-form-115.title: River channel migration, how rivers wander
soil-form-115.text: An alluvial river never stays put. River channel migration is the sideways shift of its channel across its floodplain over time. Bank erosion drives it, combined with point bar deposition, the building of a sediment bar, on the opposite side of the channel. Around each bend, water moves in a corkscrew-like helicoidal flow. It undercuts banks into cut banks and moves sediment across the channel. Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank, so meanders become better defined over time. The typical features are point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

soil-form-114.title: Stone stripes, bands of rock sorted by frost
soil-form-114.text: Bare bands of broken basalt streak the hillsides of north central Oregon. A stone stripe, or lava stringer, is an elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff. Most lie at 900 to 1,100 m. Each runs a few metres to over 150 m long, 0.3 to 3 m wide and 20 to 65 cm deep. They probably formed in the near-glacial cold of the Quaternary, through frost action, surface erosion, the washing down of fine material and slow downhill movement under gravity. Intense freeze–thaw cycles likely sorted the rock debris. Frost reached no deeper than about 1 m, which explains their shallowness. On level ground the same processes form stone rings around soil mounds, and these grade into stripes as the slope steepens.

openers.form: Beneath every field lies solid rock, and over it lies a blanket of loose material that soil grows in. That blanket can be rock rotted in place by long chemical weathering, or debris moved by water, wind, ice or gravity. Rivers spread clay, silt, sand and gravel across floodplains. Wind piles up silt-sized dust, and rainwash and creep gather loose sediment at the foot of hillslopes. This part of the course follows soil from those raw materials to the layered bodies they become, and it begins with the rock and loose cover themselves.
openers.weathering-and-parent-material: Soil does not start from nothing. It forms in an underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a loose surface deposit, that it inherits much from. Some of that material is rock weathered in place, so deeply that geologists call it rotten rock. Much more was carried in and is classified by how it last traveled. This chapter sorts those materials, from silt-sized wind-blown dust to the loose cover of asteroids and the icy ground of Saturn's moon Titan.

reviews.weathering-and-parent-material: Soil begins where bedrock gives way to regolith, the loose blanket that covers rock on Earth and on other worlds. Part of that blanket is rock weathered in place: saprolite keeps its bedrock's structure, residuum has lost it, and deep weathering builds such profiles over millions of years in stable, warm, humid lands. Most soils, though, grow in material that wind, water, ice or gravity carried in. Each carrier leaves a signature: well-sorted alluvium, poorly sorted colluvium, unsorted till, silty loess and fine lake clays. Whatever its origin, the parent material passes on much of a soil's structure and minerals, so shale gives clay-rich soils and sandstone gives sandy ones.
